title: Inventory-first reservation allocator model and sensitivity workbook
summary: A compact spreadsheet-style model that prioritizes physical inventory (GPU count by SKU / zone) to recommend how many GPUs to reserve vs leave for spot/burst, producing slice recommendations, marginal unit economics and short-run break-even timelines under multiple scenarios.
assumptions:
- Time horizon: 12 month planning window
- Units: GPU-hours by SKU (A100-80GB, A100-40GB, L4)
- Price inputs: cloud list, committed discount bands, op-ex overhead per GPU
- Demand is expressed as expected GPU-hour curve (base, seasonal peaks) with 5th/50th/95th percentiles
- Workloads: steady-state synchronous inference (low-latency) + asynchronous batch backfills
- No cross-customer bursting across reserved pools unless explicit transfer credit is set
body:
Sheet layout (tab list):

Tab: Inputs
- inventory_by_sku (table): columns [sku, region, total_gpus, hourly_cloud_cost_per_gpu, reserved_unit_price_month, amort_months, power_and_ops_per_gpu_hour]
- demand_curve (table): columns [month, p05_gpu_hours, p50_gpu_hours, p95_gpu_hours]
- workload_profile (table): columns [workload, latency_slo_ms, pct_base_load, pct_peak_load, batch_eligible_pct]
- pricing_bands (table): columns [commit_tier_name, min_monthly_gpu_hours, discount_pct, max_volume]
- policy_flags: {sticky_reserved: yes/no, allow_cross_pool_burst: yes/no, prefer_lower_latency_zones: yes/no}

Tab: Core calculations
- Step 1 (convert demand to concurrent GPU requirement):
  formula: concurrent_gpus = ceil(gpu_hours_in_hour / 1) with smoothing window of 1 hour for low-latency. For batch, use longer smoothing window (4h).
- Step 2 (inventory-first allocator):
  iterate regions and SKUs in descending order of latency priority. For each month:
    assign reserved_gpus = min(total_gpus, baseline_concurrent_gpus * reserve_fraction)
    compute reserved_coverage_pct = reserved_gpus / peak_concurrent_gpus
- Step 3 (marginal cost calc):
  marginal_token_cost_proxy = (reserved_unit_price_month / (amort_months * avg_monthly_gpu_hours)) + power_and_ops_per_gpu_hour
  cloud_spot_cost_proxy = hourly_cloud_cost_per_gpu * (1 + spot_premium)
- Step 4 (break-even months):
  breakeven_months = (cost_to_buy_reserved - expected_spot_savings_per_month) / monthly_savings_from_reserved

Tab: Sensitivity scenarios
- Scenario A (Conservative): high base demand, low seasonal spike => reserve smaller fraction but more evenly across SKUs
- Scenario B (Aggressive reserve): moderate sustained demand, high price delta between reserved and spot => reserve larger slices and prioritize amortization length 36 months
- Scenario C (Inventory-constrained): limited available GPUs by SKU in region => shift reservations to cheaper/available SKU with cross-region replication cost added

Tab: Sample numbers (illustrative)
- inventory_by_sku example rows:
  [A100-80GB, us-west1, 120, 6.50, 2200, 36, 0.30]
  [A100-40GB, us-west1, 80, 4.20, 1400, 24, 0.25]
  [L4, us-east1, 300, 1.20, 450, 12, 0.12]

- demand_curve (month 6 p50): p50_gpu_hours = 11000 => concurrent baseline ~ 460 gpus (assuming 24h) -> smoothing reduces to 380 for inference profile

- Calculation snapshot (month 6):
  chosen_reserved_fraction = 0.65 => target_reserved_gpus = 247 (from available inventory)
  reserved_unit_price_month (weighted avg) = $1,150 -> implied marginal proxy $1,150/(36*720)= $0.044/h + ops 0.30/h => $0.344/h effective
  cloud_spot_cost_proxy (weighted) = $6.50/h * 0.9 premium factor -> $5.85/h
  monthly_savings_per_gpu = (spot - reserved_effective) * average_util_hours = (5.85 - 0.344) * 720 = $3,789 per GPU per month (illustrative)
  break_even_months for 24m amortization = cost_of_reserve / monthly_savings -> ~ 0.3 months (illustrative, indicates strong win if numbers hold)

Key output columns produced by sheet (per-month, per-region):
- recommended_reserved_count_by_sku (number)
- reserve_coverage_pct (percentage of p95)
- expected_monthly_savings_usd
- stranded_risk_index (0-1) computed from utilization variance and pool fragmentation
- suggested_rollover_action (scale_up|scale_down|no_change|reassign_sku)

Notes on stranded risk index: combine three signals 1) leftover_idle_gpu_hours_pct after expected baseline allocation 2) fragmentation_score (number of small buckets < 4gpus) 3) expected short-term demand variance (stdev/p50). Normalized and weighted (0.4,0.3,0.3). Values > 0.6 => consider flexible contracts or sellback program.

Actionable recommendations (draft):
- Near-term (next 30d): run an A/B with two reservation mixes: 60% reserve fraction focused on A100-40 + 20% L4 reserved for baseload. Track actual utilization at 1h resolution.
- 60–90d: If realized p50 > planned by 15%, increase reserved fraction by +10 pp but cap new reservations to SKU availability.
- 90–180d: For pools with stranded_risk_index > 0.7, offer internal credit incentives to migrate low-latency workloads into pooled reserved capacity or enable cross-pool transfer credits.
- Policy: prefer longer amortization for stable enterprise customers (36 months) and shorter (12 months) for volatile startup workloads.

Open questions / unknowns: 
- How quickly can we procure additional inventory in APAC for peak season? (affects inventory-first allocations)
- What is the operational overhead to reassign GPUs across pools (networking / tenancy reconfiguration)?
- Spot pricing volatility assumption: currently using 10% discount factor — validate against last 9 months of cloud invoices.

TODOs / next steps: 
- [ ] Hook live daily cloud invoice extracts into the sheet (billing->SKU mapping) 
- [ ] Add Monte Carlo sampling for demand_curve to compute P90 regret metrics
- [ ] Run small simulation (3 months) comparing existing reservation plan vs allocator outputs and capture delta in unit costs and SLO misses
- [ ] Present to pricing-steering on 2024-11-10 for decision on amortization policy

Comments: This workbook is intentionally "inventory-first" — it starts from what we can realistically reserve and recommends slices to cover the measurable base demand. It avoids optimistic demand-fitting that assumes we can buy unlimited reserved capacity. The approach trades some short-term savings for lower stranded risk and faster operational execution.
